Advertisement Advertisement The forum forms part of Wellington College International Lagos’ contribution to wider conversations on the future of education, reflecting its commitment to exploring how young people can be equipped not only to navigate technological change but also to thrive in a rapidly evolving world. Held under the theme “Human Flourishing in the Age of AI”, the forum explored how young people can flourish in an increasingly AI-enabled world, ahead of the school’s September 2027 opening at Alaro City, Lagos. Christine Haslett, founding headmaster of Wellington College International Lagos, in her address, emphasised the importance of an education that develops character, curiosity and a sense of purpose alongside academic excellence. She also highlighted the shared responsibility of educators, families and wider society in preparing young people for the future. Chris Rothwell, founding director of the Wellington College Education Institute of AI, in his keynote address, explored the changing relationship between education and artificial intelligence, and the implications for how young people learn, think and prepare for the future. Advertisement He examined the opportunities and challenges presented by increasingly capable AI systems, including the importance of developing independent thinking, creativity, sound judgement and the ability to use emerging technologies responsibly. “AI is changing not only how we work and learn, but the opportunities available to us and the choices we make. The decisions we take about education today will shape whether young people can genuinely benefit from those changes or simply struggle to keep pace with them. Advertisement “Human flourishing must therefore be central to how we prepare the next generation, not an aspiration we return to after technological progress,” he said. Anthony Seldon, founding director of Wellington College Education and one of Britain’s leading educational thinkers, historians and authors, contributed to the forum through a specially recorded address. Advertisement Advertisement He reflected on the importance of developing young people who can exercise sound judgement, adapt to change, understand themselves and others, and build meaningful human relationships in AI age. Iyinoluwa Aboyeji, founding partner at Future Africa, emphasised the need to prepare young people to identify problems, exercise initiative and create meaningful solutions. “In the age of AI, the skill that distinguishes talent is not knowing but building. Our children need to learn early what it takes to lead their peers in combining AI with deep customer insight to build real solutions to real problems. “I was delighted to share lessons from our journey building Talent Nation into one of the largest AI engineering workforces in the world,” he said. Abisola Dokunmu-Adegbite, the permanent secretary of the Lagos State Ministry of Basic and Secondary Education, represented by Oyindamola Martins, the director ICT at the ministry, in her goodwill message said: “The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence is transforming virtually every aspect of human life, and the education sector is no exception. We are witnessing a new era in which technology is reshaping how knowledge is accessed, teaching is delivered, learning is experienced, and educational outcomes are achieved. “As a ministry, we recognise that the future of education must go beyond traditional teaching and learning methods. We must embrace innovation, equip our teachers with relevant digital skills, and prepare our students with the knowledge, creativity, critical thinking, problem-solving abilities and digital competencies required to thrive in a technology-driven society.’’ Wellington College Education aims to use the forum to convene a national conversation on what it means to be an educated person in the second quarter of the twenty-first century. The college located in Alaro City, within the Lekki Free Zone, Lagos, is a premium co-educational day and boarding school scheduled to welcome students aged three–18 to its purpose-built campus from September 2027. The school is being developed to provide an environment that supports academic excellence alongside creativity, sport, the arts, wellbeing and wider student development, bringing Wellington’s distinctive educational approach to a new generation of students in Nigeria.
